datenschutz-grundprinzipien-01.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the principles listed in Art. 5(1) GDPR for processing personal data?

options.a: Data minimisation: only data that is actually necessary for the purpose may be collected
options.b: Storage limitation: data may not be kept longer than necessary
options.c: Profit maximisation: processing must serve the company's economic success
options.d: Accuracy: data must be factually correct and kept up to date where necessary

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-01.explanation: Art. 5(1) GDPR lists seven principles: lawfulness/fairness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality, plus accountability (Art. 5(2)). Economic benefit to the company is not a data protection principle in its own right - at most it can feed into a legitimate interest under Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR, but it never replaces the other duties.

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-02.question: HR has stored an employee's private email address solely to process payroll. May the marketing department simply use that address to send her advertising for internal employee perks?

options.a: Yes, once data is lawfully held anywhere in the company it may be reused for any internal purpose
options.b: No, that would violate purpose limitation - reusing data for a different purpose needs its own legal basis or a compatibility check
options.c: Yes, because this is internal communication within the same employer and GDPR only governs data shared externally
options.d: No, but only because it is a private rather than a work email address

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-02.explanation: The purpose-limitation principle (Art. 5(1)(b) GDPR) means personal data collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes may not simply be reused for an incompatible purpose. Reuse is only permitted after a compatibility assessment (Art. 6(4) GDPR) or on the strength of a new, separate legal basis - 'the company already has it' is not sufficient justification.

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-03.question: Which of the following is NOT an independent legal basis under Art. 6(1) GDPR for processing personal data?

options.a: Processing is necessary for the performance of a contract with the data subject
options.b: The data subject has validly given consent to the processing
options.c: Processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject
options.d: Processing merely makes internal workflows more convenient and saves cost

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-03.explanation: Art. 6(1) GDPR recognises six legal bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, and legitimate interest. Mere operational convenience or cost savings is not, by itself, any of these six - at most it can feed into the balancing-of-interests test under Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR, where it still has to be weighed against the data subject's interests.

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-04.question: What does the accountability principle under Art. 5(2) GDPR actually require of the controller?

options.a: They must not only comply with the data protection principles but also be able to demonstrate that compliance, e.g. through documentation, records, and policies
options.b: They must obtain prior approval from the supervisory authority for every processing activity
options.c: They must issue an annual public press release accounting for all data breaches
options.d: They must publish all processing activities for free public inspection by anyone

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-04.explanation: Accountability means it is not enough to actually comply with data protection law - the controller must also be able to prove that compliance at any time, for example through a record of processing activities (Art. 30 GDPR), internal policies, training records, or data protection impact assessments. There is no general requirement to get prior authority approval for each processing activity, and no duty to issue a public press release for every activity.

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-01.question: An employee submits a request to HR for access to the data held about them (Art. 15 GDPR). Within what timeframe must the company generally respond?

options.a: Within 72 hours, as with a data breach
options.b: Without undue delay and at the latest within one month of receiving the request; a further two-month extension is possible for complex cases, with reasons given
options.c: There is no statutory deadline - a response 'within a reasonable time' is always sufficient
options.d: Within one year, since access requests rank behind day-to-day business

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-01.explanation: Under Art. 12(3) GDPR, the controller must provide information on the action taken without undue delay and in any event within one month of receiving the request. For multiple or complex requests, this can be extended by a further two months, but the data subject must be informed of the extension within the first month. Missing the deadline is a serious compliance failure that can trigger a complaint to the supervisory authority - hence marked high_stakes.

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-02.question: A former employee, six months after leaving, demands complete deletion of her payslips (Art. 17 GDPR). How should the company respond?

options.a: Delete immediately, since every erasure request must be executed within 72 hours without exception
options.b: Refuse, because the right to erasure generally does not apply to former employees
options.c: Not fully grant the request to the extent statutory retention obligations (e.g. tax and commercial-law retention periods) prevent deletion - that data must be retained for now but restricted from other use
options.d: Delete it, but only if the former employee first provides written confirmation from the tax authority

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-02.explanation: The right to erasure under Art. 17 GDPR generally does apply to former employees too, but it is limited by Art. 17(3)(b) GDPR where processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation (e.g. commercial/tax retention periods under German commercial and tax law). In such cases the data must be kept until the retention period expires but may no longer be used for other purposes. A blanket refusal or an unchecked 72-hour deletion would both be wrong - getting this wrong is a serious compliance failure, hence high_stakes.

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-03.question: What does the 'right to data portability' under Art. 20 GDPR actually mean?

options.a: The right to have a company forward personal data to any third party without limit
options.b: The right to receive data provided to a controller - where processing is based on consent or contract and carried out by automated means - in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format, or to have it transmitted directly to another controller
options.c: The right to a free physical paper copy of all files, regardless of the legal basis for processing
options.d: The right to have data automatically transferred to a new employer after one year

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-03.explanation: Art. 20 GDPR only covers data the data subject provided themselves, where processing is based on consent or a contract and is carried out by automated means. Its purpose is to make it easier to switch between providers or services, not to create a general obligation to pass data to third parties or a right to paper copies regardless of the legal basis.

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-04.question: A customer objects to their data being processed for direct marketing purposes. How must the company respond?

options.a: Processing for marketing purposes must stop immediately and without exception - for direct marketing, the company has no 'balancing of interests' option
options.b: The company may continue the marketing if it can demonstrate an overriding legitimate interest
options.c: The company only has to honour the objection if the customer provides a justification
options.d: There is no legal right to object to marketing, only a right to withdraw a consent that was previously given

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-04.explanation: For direct marketing, the right to object under Art. 21(2) and (3) GDPR is an absolute right: as soon as the data subject objects, their data may no longer be processed for that purpose - unlike the general objection right in Art. 21(1) GDPR, there is no balancing-of-interests test here, and no justification is required from the customer.

datenschutz-datensicherheit-01.question: What does Art. 32 GDPR require of controllers and processors regarding 'technical and organisational measures' (TOMs)?

options.a: A single, fixed list of measures that applies identically to every company
options.b: A level of protection appropriate to the risk, e.g. through encryption, access controls, ensuring confidentiality/integrity/availability, and regularly testing the effectiveness of the measures
options.c: Only physical measures such as lockable filing cabinets - IT security is not covered by this article
options.d: An obligation to carry out a data protection impact assessment for every processing activity

datenschutz-datensicherheit-01.explanation: Art. 32 GDPR does not prescribe a fixed checklist but a risk-appropriate level of protection: the actual scope of measures depends on the state of the art, implementation costs, and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing as well as the risk to data subjects. It mentions, among other things, pseudonymisation/encryption, ensuring confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience, and a process for regularly testing effectiveness. A data protection impact assessment is a separate instrument under Art. 35 GDPR, not a TOM.

datenschutz-datensicherheit-02.question: A new internal applicant-tracking tool is being introduced. What does the 'privacy by design and by default' principle (Art. 25 GDPR) actually require here?

options.a: That data protection is bolted on afterwards via an update once complaints start coming in
options.b: That all available data fields are switched on by default so nothing is missing later
options.c: That only the IT department, and never business departments, is responsible for privacy settings
options.d: That data protection is built into the tool's design from the start, with the most privacy-friendly settings (e.g. minimal mandatory fields, the shortest reasonable retention periods) active by default

datenschutz-datensicherheit-02.explanation: Privacy by design means data protection requirements are built into a system's planning and development from the outset, rather than patched on afterwards. Privacy by default means that, without any active choice by the user, only the data necessary for the specific purpose is processed by default - so default settings must be privacy-friendly, not maximally data-collecting.

datenschutz-datensicherheit-03.question: Which of the following counts as a 'special category of personal data' under Art. 9(1) GDPR, requiring especially strict protection?

options.a: An employee's office number and phone extension
options.b: An employee's monthly gross salary
options.c: Information about an employee's trade union membership or state of health
options.d: An employee's home address and private mobile number

datenschutz-datensicherheit-03.explanation: Art. 9(1) GDPR lists, among others, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic and biometric data, health data, and data concerning a person's sex life or sexual orientation as special categories. Salary, office numbers, or contact details are protectable personal data too, but they do not fall into this heightened-protection category - mishandling confidentiality for genuinely sensitive health or union data is a serious violation, hence high_stakes.

datenschutz-datensicherheit-04.question: An employee submits a doctor's note to HR to prove sick leave. On what basis may the employer process this health data, given that it is specially protected?

options.a: Employee health data may never be processed under any circumstances, not even for sick-leave certificates
options.b: Processing is permitted because it is necessary for exercising rights and obligations arising from the employment relationship (Art. 9(2)(b) GDPR in conjunction with §26 BDSG); access should be limited to what is strictly necessary
options.c: Only with a notarised consent form from the employee - a statutory basis is not sufficient here
options.d: Only if the employee's health insurance provider grants the employer prior authorisation to process it

datenschutz-datensicherheit-04.explanation: Art. 9(2)(b) GDPR permits processing special categories of data where necessary for exercising rights and obligations under employment and social security law; §26 BDSG spells this out for German employment relationships. Sick notes are a classic, everyday example - consent is not strictly required here, but access should still be limited to a small number of authorised people (typically HR) under a need-to-know principle.

datenschutz-meldepflichten-01.question: On Monday morning, IT discovers that on Friday evening a database of customer data was briefly accessible unencrypted on the internet, and a risk to data subjects' rights is likely. By when must the incident generally be reported to the competent supervisory authority?

options.a: Only at the end of the current quarter, as part of the regular data protection report
options.b: Without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of the company becoming aware of it (not from the moment the incident itself occurred); if the deadline is missed, a justification for the delay must be provided
options.c: Within 72 hours of the actual moment the breach occurred, regardless of when it was discovered
options.d: There is no notification duty unless credit card data is involved

datenschutz-meldepflichten-01.explanation: The 72-hour deadline under Art. 33(1) GDPR starts running once the controller becomes aware of the breach - not from the actual moment the incident occurred, which may go unnoticed for a while. If the notification cannot be made in time, it must still be made without further delay, accompanied by reasons for the delay. Missing this deadline without good reason is a serious compliance failure, hence high_stakes.

datenschutz-meldepflichten-02.question: An employee briefly loses a fully encrypted company laptop that can immediately be remote-locked and wiped; no one accessed the data in the meantime. Must this incident be reported to the supervisory authority?

options.a: Not necessarily - if the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects (e.g. because of effective encryption and remote wipe), the notification duty under Art. 33(1) GDPR does not apply, though the incident should still be documented internally
options.b: Yes, every data breach without exception must be reported to the supervisory authority
options.c: No, a notification duty only exists for cyberattacks by third parties, never for lost devices
options.d: Yes, but only if the laptop was missing for more than 72 hours

datenschutz-meldepflichten-02.explanation: Art. 33(1) GDPR provides an exception to the notification duty to the supervisory authority where the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. Effective encryption and immediate remote wiping can substantially reduce such a risk. Importantly, even breaches that don't need to be reported must still be documented internally under Art. 33(5) GDPR, so the supervisory authority can review compliance if needed.

datenschutz-meldepflichten-03.question: In a cyberattack, unencrypted health data and social security numbers of several thousand customers are stolen, likely posing a high risk to those affected. Is it enough to report this incident only to the supervisory authority?

options.a: Yes, notifying the supervisory authority under Art. 33 GDPR automatically also covers informing the data subjects
options.b: No, affected individuals only need to be informed if they proactively ask the company about it
options.c: No, where a high risk is likely, the affected individuals must additionally be notified without undue delay under Art. 34 GDPR, unless one of the exceptions in Art. 34(3) GDPR applies (e.g. the affected data was effectively encrypted)
options.d: No, but notifying affected individuals is only required after a regulatory fine proceeding has concluded

datenschutz-meldepflichten-03.explanation: Art. 33 GDPR (notifying the supervisory authority) and Art. 34 GDPR (notifying data subjects) are two separate duties with different thresholds: Art. 33 already applies at any risk level, while Art. 34 only kicks in where a high risk is likely - and then it applies in addition to, not instead of, the authority notification. Exceptions under Art. 34(3) GDPR apply where the data was effectively encrypted, where subsequent measures have eliminated the high risk, or where individual notification would involve disproportionate effort (then public communication can substitute). Unencrypted stolen health data is a textbook high-risk case - failing to notify would be a serious violation, hence high_stakes.

datenschutz-meldepflichten-04.question: After reviewing a minor incident, the company decides there is no duty to notify the supervisory authority because no risk to data subjects is apparent. Is the matter then closed?

options.a: Yes, without a notification duty, all further obligations regarding this incident disappear entirely
options.b: No, under Art. 33(5) GDPR, every personal data breach - including the facts, its effects, and the remedial action taken - must still be documented internally so the supervisory authority can verify compliance
options.c: No, all of the company's customers must nevertheless be informed as a precaution
options.d: Yes, documentation is only required for incidents that are subject to the notification duty

datenschutz-meldepflichten-04.explanation: Art. 33(5) GDPR requires controllers to document every personal data breach, regardless of whether notification to the supervisory authority is required. This documentation serves as evidence of accountability and allows the supervisory authority to review the company's risk assessment after the fact. Blanket notification of all customers is not required where no risk exists and would only cause unnecessary alarm.

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-01.question: The company wants to outsource payroll processing to an external service provider, who needs access to employee data for this. What is mandatory before the provider may begin processing?

options.a: An informal verbal agreement is enough, as long as both sides trust each other
options.b: A written (electronic form is acceptable) data processing agreement under Art. 28 GDPR, covering, among other things, the subject matter, duration, nature and purpose of processing, categories of data, and the processor's obligations
options.c: Notarisation of the arrangement, because employee data is involved
options.d: Nothing, as long as the service provider is also based in Germany

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-01.explanation: Art. 28(9) GDPR mandates a written contract for data processing on behalf of a controller (electronic form is sufficient). Under Art. 28(3) GDPR, the contract must set out, among other things, the subject matter, duration, nature and purpose of processing, the type of personal data and categories of data subjects, and the obligations and rights of the controller. A purely verbal trust-based arrangement is not enough, regardless of where the service provider is located.

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-02.question: An engaged IT service provider wants to bring in a further subcontractor (sub-processor) for data storage. May it simply do so?

options.a: No, under Art. 28(2) GDPR a processor may not engage another processor without the controller's prior specific or general written authorisation
options.b: Yes, once a contract with the main service provider exists, any number of further subcontractors can be brought in without additional authorisation
options.c: Yes, as long as the subcontractor is based within the EU, no separate authorisation is needed
options.d: No, sub-processors are generally prohibited under GDPR

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-02.explanation: Art. 28(2) GDPR requires that a processor does not engage another processor without the controller's prior specific or general written authorisation. Where a general authorisation is given, the processor must inform the controller of intended changes so the controller can object. Being based within the EU doesn't remove this authorisation requirement, and sub-processors are not banned outright - they are simply subject to conditions.

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-03.question: A company wants to transfer customer data to a cloud provider based outside the EU/EEA. What applies here, at a conceptual level, under Art. 44 et seq. GDPR?

options.a: Such a transfer is fundamentally prohibited and never permitted
options.b: It is always enough that the customer gave prior consent by email, regardless of the destination country
options.c: The transfer needs a suitable basis, e.g. an adequacy decision by the European Commission for the destination country (Art. 45 GDPR) or appropriate safeguards such as EU Standard Contractual Clauses (Art. 46 GDPR); without such a basis, the transfer is generally not permitted
options.d: Such transfers are governed solely by the destination country's national law, not by GDPR

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-03.explanation: Transfers of personal data to third countries are only permitted under Art. 44 GDPR if a suitable basis exists: either an adequacy decision by the European Commission confirming an adequate level of protection in the destination country (Art. 45 GDPR), or appropriate safeguards such as EU Standard Contractual Clauses, binding corporate rules, or, in narrow cases, one of the derogations listed in Art. 49 GDPR. A simple email consent generally isn't sufficient as the sole, ongoing basis for regular transfers, and GDPR applies in addition to the destination country's national law, not instead of it.

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-04.question: As part of onboarding, a new employee is given access to a system containing customer data, even though their role only requires part of that data. Which principle is being violated here, and what is the correct approach?

options.a: No principle is violated, since every employee should generally have access to all company data
options.b: This is a violation of the right to data portability, since the employee could theoretically export the data
options.c: It is unproblematic as long as the employee has been bound to confidentiality under §53 BDSG, regardless of the scope of their access rights
options.d: This violates the need-to-know principle; access rights should be restricted, under the data minimisation principle, to what is actually required for the employee's task, in addition to the general duty of confidentiality under §53 BDSG

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-04.explanation: Beyond the general duty of employees to maintain confidentiality under §53 BDSG, the data minimisation principle (Art. 5(1)(c) GDPR) requires that access rights be granted on a need-to-know basis: employees should only be able to access the data actually required for their specific task. A confidentiality obligation does not substitute for technical access restrictions - both are required, not one or the other.
